title: Resources
text:
Definitions from Glosario
Further definitions at Glosario
Argument: one of possibly several expressions that are passed to a function. Oftentimes parameter and arugument are used interchangably, even though techincally parameter refers to the variable and argument refers to the value.
Assignment operator: Symbol that assigns values on the right to an object on the left. Looks like <-. Keyboard shortcut is Alt + -
Comment: Text written in a script that is not treated as code to be run, but rather as text that describes what the code is doing. These are usually short notes, beginning with a #
Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN): A public repository of R packages.
Data frame: A two-dimensional data structure for storing tabular data in memory. Rows represent records and columns represent variables.
Function: A code block which gathers a sequence of operations into a whole, preserving it for ongoing use by defining a set of tasks that takes zero or more required and optional arguments as inputs and returns expected outputs (return values), if any. Functions enable repeating these defined tasks with one command, known as a function call.
NA: A special value used to represent data that is not available.
Pipe operator: The %>% used to make the output of one function the input of the next.
Package: A collection of code, data, and documentation that can be distributed and re-used. Also referred to in some languages as a library or module.
Parameter: A variable specified in a function definition whose value is passed to the function when the function is called. Parameters and arguments are distinct, but related concepts. Parameters are variables and arguments are the values assigned to those variables. In practice though these terms are often used interchangeably.
Positional argument: An argument to a function that gets its value according to its place in the function’s definition, as opposed to a named argument that is explicitly matched by name.
Reproducible research: The practice of describing and documenting research results in such a way that another researcher or person can re-run the analysis code on the same data to obtain the same result.
Tibble: A modern replacement for R’s data frame, which stores tabular data in columns and rows, defined and used in the tidyverse. Almost always when you are working with a data frame, you are actually working with a tibble.
Tidy data: Tabular data that satisfies three conditions that facilitate initial cleaning, and later exploration and analysis—(1) each variable forms a column, (2) each observation forms a row, and (3) each type of observation unit forms a table.
Tidyverse: A collection of R packages for operating on tabular data in consistent ways.
Variable: A name in a program that has some data associated with it. A variable’s value can be changed after definition.
Vector: A sequence of values that have all the same type. Vectors are the fundamental data structure in R; a scalar is just a vector with exactly one element.

title: Group Project
text: Each group picks a question about one of two new datasets, works on it over two mornings, and on Friday presents to a group that worked on the other dataset. We do not give you an answer to check against.

title: Group Project
text:
Groups and schedule
There are ten groups of six people. Five groups (A1 to A5) take Study A and five (B1 to B5) take Study B. You meet your group on Wednesday morning.
On Friday each Study A group pairs with the Study B group of the same number and sits with them. A1 presents to B1, then B1 presents to A1; A2 and B2 do the same nearby, and so on. Your audience has spent two mornings on a different dataset, so explain your study before your result.








when
how long
what




Wednesday AM
3 hours
meet, read the data, agree a question, first analysis: Tuesday’s ordination and PERMANOVA are a good place to start


Thursday AM
3 hours
add Wednesday’s differential tests, finish the analysis, build the figures, write the talk


Friday AM
30 minutes
final preparation


Friday AM
1 hour
present to your paired group for 30 minutes, then listen to theirs for 30



Both datasets have exactly the file layout you have been using all week, with the same column names. Your code from the modules should run on them with the file path changed and nothing else.
source("R/count_tables.R")
d <- read_counts("group_a")   # or "group_b"

title: Group Project
section: Study A: does a vaginal probiotic change the community?
text:
Study A: does a vaginal probiotic change the community?
A randomised trial. Participants received either a live Lactobacillus crispatus product or a placebo, and were sampled before and after the course of treatment.







participants
176


samples
352, one before and one after per person


arms
121 probiotic, 55 placebo


metadata
arm, time_point (pre, post), age, pH, Nugent score, Amsel criteria



The obvious question is whether the product changed the bacterial community, and whether it changed host gene expression.
There are less obvious ones. Did it work in everyone, or only in people whose community was already a particular way before treatment? Does the host response track the community change, or move on its own? Is a difference after treatment meaningful if the two arms already differed before it?
The arms are unbalanced, 121 against 55, so check your baseline before you interpret anything about the follow-up.
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Group Project
section: Study B: do hormonal contraceptives differ in their effect?
text:
Study B: do hormonal contraceptives differ in their effect?
A cross-sectional comparison of three contraceptive methods, each person sampled once.







participants
93, one sample each


arms
39 injectable, 28 pill, 26 ring


metadata
arm, bv (Amsel), nugent, ph, any_sti



The obvious question is whether the three methods differ in bacterial community composition, in host gene expression, or in both.
Then the less obvious ones. One of the three methods is delivered locally and two are systemic. Does that grouping explain more than the three-way split does? Is bacterial vaginosis more common in one arm, and if so is that the explanation for everything else you find? With 93 samples and three groups, which of your comparisons is actually powered?
Keep in mind that the study is cross-sectional. Nobody was randomised to a method, and people who choose different methods differ in other ways.

title: Group Project
text:
Deliverables
A presentation that fits your 30-minute slot, containing:

the question you settled on, in one sentence
what you did, including what you filtered and why
two or three figures, each with a caption you read out
the answer, stated as plainly as the data allow
what you do not believe about your own result

The last of these is required. When you are the audience, ask the other group about theirs. Every analysis this week had something wrong with it, so look for the problems in yours before you present.

title: Group Project
text:
Advice from the modules






TipThings that bit people earlier in the week




Check your sample table and your count matrix are in the same order before you run any test.
Decide your filter before you look at the result, and write down why.
On a species table, give DESeq2 poscounts size factors and check how many species they were built from.
Define a grouping from one table and test the other, never the same table twice.
Look at how lopsided a ranking is before you believe an enrichment.
Your dataset has an rnaseq_batch column. Cross-tabulate it against your groups early, and find out whether you have a confound rather than a finding.

Using the agent
Use Pi as much as you like. It writes most code faster than you can, and groups that use it well tend to get further.
At some point this week it will also give you an answer that is confident and wrong. Before any number goes on a slide, one person in the group who did not write the code should be able to say where it came from.
Divide the work: someone drives the analysis, someone checks it, someone builds the figures, someone writes the talk. Swap at least once.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
Does combining two measurements tell you anything that neither told you alone? This module shows how to check, surveys the integration methods, and argues that the simplest one is the baseline the others have to beat.
This module is a lecture and a discussion. There is no coding exercise. The second half of the morning is your group presentations, given to one paired group rather than the whole room.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
Running the analysis yourself
Nothing in this module is assessed, but the code behind every number on the slides is short enough to read. The whole analysis is three logistic regressions on a table with four columns.
library(tidyverse)
library(pROC)

# one row per participant: micro_z, host_z, preterm
per_person <- read_csv("per_person_scores.csv")

fits <- list(
  micro = glm(preterm ~ micro_z, per_person, family = binomial),
  host  = glm(preterm ~ host_z,  per_person, family = binomial),
  both  = glm(preterm ~ micro_z + host_z, per_person, family = binomial)
)

map_dbl(fits, ~ as.numeric(auc(roc(per_person$preterm, predict(.x), quiet = TRUE))))
anova(fits$micro, fits$both, test = "Chisq")
The two scores come from Tuesday and Thursday. One is the mean anaerobe fraction per person from the species table, the other the mean inflammatory gene set score per person from the gene table.

title: Sets and Enrichment
section: Exercise 1: From a gene list to a sentence
text:
Exercise 1: From a gene list to a sentence
Open notebooks/05-enrichment.qmd. You need yesterday’s preterm-versus-term results for the gene table, from step 7 of Module 4’s second exercise. If you no longer have them, rerun the three lines that made them.

Part 1: Predict

You are about to test 50 gene sets. If none were truly enriched, how many would come out with padj < 0.05?
Your preterm-versus-term gene list had 838 genes up and 860 down, which is almost perfectly balanced. Does that make you more or less willing to believe an enrichment result?
Name one biological program you expect to be elevated in the people who delivered preterm. You will check this against the answer.



Part 2: Build

Build the ranking vector from your outcome results: res$stat, named by gene, with missing values dropped. How many genes are in it?
Get the Hallmark sets:
hallmark <- msigdbr::msigdbr(species = "Homo sapiens", collection = "H")
sets <- split(hallmark$ensembl_gene, hallmark$gs_name)
Check that the identifiers in sets are the same kind as the names of your ranking vector. If one is Ensembl and the other is a symbol, nothing will match, and fgsea will return almost nothing without raising an error.
Run fgsea(sets, stat, minSize = 15, maxSize = 500). Sort by padj. How many sets are significant, and how many point in each direction?
Plot the top twelve as a bar chart of NES, coloured by direction.
Check for imbalance. What share of your ranking statistic is positive? What is its mean? Now do the same for your anaerobe-versus-Lactobacillus ranking, and run fgsea on that too. Compare the two in a small table: genes up, genes down, sets significant, sets pointing one way.
Write one sentence saying which of the two enrichment results you trust and why.
Take the leading edge of your top set. Map those Ensembl identifiers to symbols with 05_gene_annotation.csv and read the list. Plot normalised counts for two of them by outcome.



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi to run the enrichment. Then ask how many of your genes matched into any set at all. An identifier mismatch is the most common failure here, and it fails silently with plausible-looking output.
Ask it to interpret the top five sets. It will write a confident paragraph about inflammation and preterm birth. Ask it which of those five sets share genes with each other. Overlapping sets are not independent findings.
Ask it whether your result could be an artifact of the ranking being lopsided. See whether it checks or just reassures you.
Ask it for the hypergeometric version using only your significant genes. Compare the two answers. Where they disagree, work out which is throwing away information.



Discussion

Was your Part 1 prediction of the elevated program right?
Two of the top sets overlap heavily. How would you report them without double counting?
Yesterday preterm against term gave you 1,698 genes and no clear story; today it gives you one sentence. What did enrichment add, and what did it hide?
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Sets and Enrichment
section: Exercise 2: The same function, on 53 species
text:
Exercise 2: The same function, on 53 species
Same notebook. You will now use the identical fgsea() call on a table with 53 features instead of 13,738, with sets built from taxonomy instead of curation.

Part 1: Predict

A gene set holds about 200 genes. A genus in our table holds between 2 and 12 species. What does that do to your ability to detect enrichment?
Which genus do you expect to come out associated with preterm birth?
Will testing ten genus sets need as aggressive a multiple-testing correction as testing fifty gene sets?



Part 2: Build

Take your species-by-outcome DESeq2 results from yesterday, the poscounts version. Build the ranking vector from stat as before.
Join 03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv so each species carries its Genus and Family.
Build the sets:
genus_sets <- split(results$feature, results$Genus)
genus_sets <- genus_sets[lengths(genus_sets) >= 2]
How many genus sets do you have? How many species are in the largest?
Run fgsea(genus_sets, species_stat, minSize = 2, maxSize = 50). Which genera are significant?
Repeat with Family instead of Genus. Does the answer agree? Check whether the top family contains the top genus.
Now do it the simple way. Just sort your 53 species by stat and print the table with genus labels. Would you have reached the same conclusion without any enrichment analysis at all?
Write two or three sentences in your notebook answering: for which of our two tables was set-based analysis worth doing, and what feature of the table decides that?



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi to build the genus sets. Then check that no species appears in two sets, and that the set sizes sum to no more than the number of species you ranked.
Species with a missing genus become a set called NA if you are careless. Check whether that happened.
Ask Pi whether enrichment analysis was useful on the species table. Then ask it to defend the opposite position. Compare the two answers and decide which argument is stronger.



Part 4: Reach (optional)
Invent a better set definition for the species table. Rather than taxonomy, group species by something functional: whether they are Lactobacillus or not, whether they are strict anaerobes, whether they are on a published list of BV-associated organisms.
Run fgsea with your hand-built sets. A set definition that encodes real biology can beat a taxonomic one, and designing such sets is research in its own right.


Discussion

The top genus is the one every clinician would have guessed, even though it does not pass. Is that reassuring, or a sign the analysis added nothing?
Taxonomy is a hierarchy and gene sets are a flat list. Does that difference matter for how you correct for multiple testing?
This is the last single-table module. Tomorrow we put the two tables together. Before you leave, write down what you think combining them could tell you that neither told you alone.
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Differential Testing
section: Exercise 1: Test the gene table with a grouping from the species table
text:
Exercise 1: Test the gene table with a grouping from the species table
Open notebooks/04-differential.qmd. Start by reading back the per-sample table you saved yesterday, the one with lacto_fraction and community in it. If you did not save it, rebuild it now; the slides from Module 2 have the recipe.

Part 1: Predict

We will test 13,738 genes. If no gene were truly different between the two community types, how many would come out with a raw p-value below 0.05?
You will test at week 18 only, which is 157 samples, 37 against 120. Would you rather have 157 samples at one visit or 471 samples across three visits? Say why before you look at anything.
Of the genes that do come out significant, do you expect more to be higher in anaerobe-dominant samples or in Lactobacillus-dominant samples?



Part 2: Build

Subset both the metadata and the gene counts to time_point == "week_18". Confirm you have 157 samples and that the column order of the count matrix matches the row order of the sample table. If they don’t match, DESeq2 gives you nonsense without any warning.
Filter the genes. Keep a gene if it has a count of at least 10 in at least a quarter of the samples.
Run the three lines:
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, sample_table, ~ community)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("community", "anaerobe", "lactobacillus"))
How many genes have padj < 0.05? How many of those have an absolute log2FoldChange above 1?
Join 05_gene_annotation.csv so your results carry gene symbols rather than Ensembl identifiers. Sort by padj and read the top twenty names out loud to your group.
Draw a volcano plot: log2FoldChange on x, -log10(padj) on y, coloured by whether the gene passed.
Pick the single top gene and plot its normalised counts as a boxplot by community. The direction of that plot must match the sign of its log2FoldChange. Check that it does.



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi how many genes were significant. Then ask it how many genes went into the test. If it can’t give you both numbers, it doesn’t know what it ran.
Ask it to explain the sign convention of your contrast. Then verify against the boxplot from step 7. Getting the direction backwards is the most common error in this analysis, and it regularly gets through peer review.
Ask it for the number of genes with pvalue < 0.05 as well as padj < 0.05. The first number should be far larger. If it is not, something is wrong.
Ask it to run the same test on CPM-normalised counts instead of raw counts. It will probably do it. Look at what happens to the results and work out why that is wrong.



Discussion

Did the direction of the effect surprise you?
What do the top genes have in common? You do not need to know the genes; read the names in gene_name and describe the pattern in plain words.
Someone will have used all 471 samples instead of 157. What is wrong with that, and how wrong is it?
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Differential Testing
section: Exercise 2: The same test, on the species table
text:
Exercise 2: The same test, on the species table
This is the second half of the same notebook. You run the same three lines of code on the 220-row species table instead of the 14,226-row gene table, with a grouping that comes from the clinic rather than from either count table.

Part 1: Predict

Why can you not test the species table using the community column you built yesterday? Answer in one sentence.
You will test species against birth outcome. The species table has 220 rows, but most are nearly always absent. How many do you expect to survive a filter of “present in at least 10% of samples”? Of those, how many are present in every one of the 157 samples?
If any species come out significant, do you expect them to be higher in the preterm group or the term group?



Part 2: Build

Subset to time_point == "week_18" again. Filter the species table to features present in at least 10% of samples.
Run the same three lines with design = ~ outcome and contrast = c("outcome", "preterm", "term"). How many species are significant?
Look at how DESeq2 normalised the samples. Count the species with no zero in any sample, sum(rowSums(counts == 0) == 0). Then plot sizeFactors(dds) against each sample’s L. iners share, both on log scales. What are the size factors really measuring?
Run it again with size factors built for a table full of zeros:
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(counts, sample_table, ~ outcome)
dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds, type = "poscounts")
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("outcome", "preterm", "term"))
How many species are significant now? Keep this version for the rest of the exercise and for tomorrow.
Join 03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv so you have readable names, and list the top ten species by padj with their fold changes, whether or not any pass. How many of the ten lean toward preterm?
Plot the relative abundance of the top three species by outcome. Use proportions, not raw counts, and consider a log scale.
Now run the test a second way, on the gene table, with the same ~ outcome design. Compare the two result sets:

how many features were tested in each
how many were significant in each
what share of the significant ones changed by more than a factor of two

Save these gene results. Tomorrow’s enrichment module starts from them.
Write down what that comparison tells you about where the outcome signal lives.



Part 3: Check the agent

A filter on a sparse table is easy to get wrong. Ask Pi how many species it kept and recompute that number yourself from rowMeans(counts > 0).
Ask it whether DESeq2 is an appropriate method for microbiome counts. Read its answer critically. Researchers disagree about this, so a confident one-sided answer is a warning sign.
Ask Pi how DESeq2 computed the size factors for the species table, and how many species went into them. Check its answer against your count from step 3.
Ask it to name the top species. Then check two of them against 03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv by hand. Agents invent plausible species names.
Ask it to also run the test with ~ nugent >= 7 as the grouping instead of outcome. Fewer samples have a Nugent score, so the sample count drops. Make sure it tells you that it dropped samples.



Part 4: Reach (optional)
Run your species-by-outcome analysis on all 471 samples, with each participant appearing three times. Compare the number of significant species to your 157-sample result.
More samples gave you more hits. Are they real? What assumption did you break?


Discussion

The default size factors gave a list of species that anyone who works on bacterial vaginosis would recognise. Why is a familiar-looking list not evidence that the method was right?
One group found many more hits in the gene table than the species table, and another found the reverse depending on their filter. What does that say about how much of a differential analysis is decided before the test runs?
At week 18 the gene table shows an outcome signal and the species table, one species at a time, does not. Does that mean the bacteria do not matter for preterm birth? What other way of looking at the species table could still find a signal?
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Distances and Ordination
section: Exercise 1: Distances and ordination on the species table
text:
Exercise 1: Distances and ordination on the species table
Open notebooks/03-ordination.qmd.

Part 1: Predict

Bray-Curtis uses abundances. Jaccard uses only presence and absence. Our species table is about 89% zeros. Which of the two do you expect to separate the two community types more clearly, and why?
If you shuffled the outcome label randomly across all 471 samples, what R2 would PERMANOVA report? Give a number.
One sample has 438 reads. Where do you expect it to sit in a Bray-Curtis ordination?



Part 2: Build

Build the phyloseq object for the species table:
library(microViz)
source("R/count_tables.R")
ps <- as_counts(table = "microbiome")
Inspect it. How many taxa, how many samples, how many sample variables? Add the community column you built this morning if it is not already there.
Run the pipeline three times, changing only the transform and the distance:

"identity" with "bray"
"binary" with "jaccard"
"clr" with "euclidean"

Plot all three, coloured by community. Put them side by side.
Colour your Bray-Curtis ordination by outcome instead. Then by time_point. Then by nugent.
Run dist_permanova() on the Bray-Curtis distance with community, outcome, time_point and rnaseq_batch as variables. Report the R2 for each.
Find your 438-read sample in the ordination. Was your Part 1 prediction right? Re-run the Bray-Curtis ordination with that sample removed and see whether anything else moves.
Make a stacked bar plot of community composition with comp_barplot(tax_level = "Genus", n_taxa = 10), faceted or ordered by community. Most 16S papers open with this figure.



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi for the R2 of outcome. Then ask it what the R2 of a random label would be. If it does not say “close to zero but not zero”, push back.
PERMANOVA with by = "margin" and by = "terms" give different answers when variables are correlated. Ask Pi which it used and why it matters.
Ask it to interpret your ordination. It will produce a paragraph of confident biological narrative about axis 1. Then ask it what axis 1 actually is. Neither it nor you can tell from the plot alone.
Ask it whether your three distance choices “agree”. Then look at the three plots yourself and decide if its answer matches what you see.



Discussion

Which of the three distances would you publish? Defend it in one sentence.
community explains a very large share of this table. Is that a finding?
Your ordination shows visit structure. Each participant appears three times. Does PERMANOVA know that, and does it matter?
crumbs: 2. Multiomics: Microbiome and Host Gene Expression

title: Distances and Ordination
section: Exercise 2: The identical pipeline on 14,000 genes
text:
Exercise 2: The identical pipeline on 14,000 genes
Use the same notebook. Change three words in your code from Exercise 1 and run it again on a table sixty times larger.

Part 1: Predict

Bray-Curtis is standard for microbiome data. Would you use it on gene counts? Say why or why not before you try.
community explained about 18% of the species table. What share do you expect it to explain of the gene table?
The gene table was produced in two sequencing batches. What share do you expect rnaseq_batch to explain?



Part 2: Build

Build the gene object, filtering as you go:
ps_genes <- as_counts(table = "rnaseq", min_count = 10, min_samples = 100)
Run the pipeline with "clr" and "euclidean", aggregating at rank = "symbol". Plot it coloured by community, then outcome, then rnaseq_batch.
Run dist_permanova() with the same four variables you used on the species table. Put the two sets of R2 values side by side in one small table.
Look at the batch row. Then do something about it: add rnaseq_batch to the PERMANOVA formula before outcome and see whether the outcome R2 changes.
Check whether batch is confounded with anything you care about. A cross-tabulation of rnaseq_batch against outcome and against community is enough. If the groups were unbalanced across batches, what would that mean for tomorrow’s differential tests, which compare the groups one gene at a time?
Also try Bray-Curtis on the gene table, just to see. Compare it to your CLR ordination and decide which you believe.



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi to compare the species and gene R2 tables and tell you what it means. Its answer will probably say the gene table has “weaker biological signal”. That is a claim about biology drawn from an ordination. Is it justified? An ordination summarises every gene at once. Tomorrow you test them one at a time, so write down what you expect to find and check it then.
Ask it whether you should remove the batch effect. Then ask it to actually do it. Look closely at what it does, because “batch correction” covers several very different operations with very different consequences.
CLR cannot handle zeros without a pseudocount. Ask Pi what pseudocount it used and where that choice came from.



Part 4: Reach (optional)
Take the first two axes of your gene ordination and the first two of your species ordination, and plot gene axis 1 against species axis 1 for the same samples. Are they related?
This scatter plot is the simplest form of multiomics integration. Friday morning starts from it.


Discussion

Both tables showed a significant outcome effect of about 2% or less. Would you write that in a paper, and how would you phrase it?
The batch effect is as large as the biological effect. What should the people who generated this data have done differently?
You now have two ordinations of the same 471 samples. What would it take to combine them, and what would you hope to gain?

title: Count Table Anatomy
text:
Exercise 1: Inside the two files

Working with the agent: Pi is in your Codespace for every exercise this week, so use it. Each exercise ends with a part that asks you to check what it produced. The habit we most want you to build is catching a confident wrong answer.

Open notebooks/02-count-table-anatomy.qmd.

Part 1: Predict, before you run anything
Write your answers down. You will compare them to the real numbers in Part 2.

The species table has 220 rows. In a single cervicovaginal sample, how many of those 220 species do you expect to see at all? Ten? Fifty? Two hundred?
The gene table has 14,226 rows. Same question.
Which table do you expect to have more zeros, as a fraction of its cells?
One sample in the species table has 438 total reads. The median is about 28,700. What do you expect to be wrong with that sample’s numbers?



Part 2: Build

Read 01_metadata.csv, 02_microbiome_counts.csv and 04_rnaseq_counts.csv.gz. Confirm that both count tables have a column for every sample_id in the metadata, and that the first column of each count file is the feature name rather than a sample.
Turn each count table into a matrix with features as row names, then compute for every sample:

library_size, the column total
features_detected, the number of rows above zero
zero_fraction, the share of rows that are zero
top_feature_share, the largest single value divided by the column total

Put those four numbers for both tables into one tidy data frame with a table column saying "species" or "genes". Keep both tables in one data frame, because every plot after this facets by table.
Plot library_size for both tables. You will need a log scale. Then plot features_detected against library_size, faceted by table.
Find the sample with 438 bacterial reads. Look at its full column. How many species does it show? What is its top_feature_share?



Part 3: Check the agent
Ask Pi to compute the four summaries for you if you have not already. Then, before you believe any of it:

Do the library sizes it reports match sum() of a column you pick by hand?
features_detected should never exceed the number of rows in the table. Is that true for every sample in its output?
Does its data frame have 942 rows, 471 samples for each of two tables? If it has 471, it dropped one of the tables without saying so.
Ask it: “which samples should I drop and why?” Then ask it what happens to your results if you keep them. See whether the second answer contradicts the first.



Discussion

Which of your Part 1 predictions was furthest off?
Someone in the room will have decided to drop the 438-read sample and someone will have kept it. Both can defend it. What does each choice cost you?
The gene table detects over 98% of its features in nearly every sample. Does that mean all 14,226 genes are expressed, or does it mean something about how the table was built?

title: Count Table Anatomy
section: Exercise 2: Filtering, normalising, and one column you will need all week
text:
Exercise 2: Filtering, normalising, and one column you will need all week
Same notebook, second half.

Part 1: Predict

If you keep only species present in at least 10% of samples, how many of the 220 survive? What share of all the bacterial reads do you lose?
Apply the same 10% prevalence rule to the 14,226 genes. How many survive?
You want to compare one species between two samples. Name the single operation you must do to the counts first.



Part 2: Build

Compute prevalence for every feature in both tables, the share of samples where its count is above zero. Plot the distribution for each table.
For prevalence cutoffs from 0 to 0.9, compute how many features survive and what share of total counts survives. Plot both. This figure shows that a prevalence filter suits one table and does almost nothing to the other.
Choose and apply a filter to each table. Write one sentence in your notebook justifying each choice. For the gene table, filter on expression level rather than prevalence, something like a mean CPM of at least 5.
Convert both filtered tables to counts per million, then to log2(cpm + 1). Plot a histogram of one feature before and after.
Build the grouping column. From the species table, compute for each sample the fraction of its reads that belong to the genus Lactobacillus. 03_microbiome_taxonomy.csv tells you which species those are.
Then make a two-level column:

lactobacillus if that fraction is 0.5 or more
anaerobe if it is below 0.5

Save your per-sample table, including sample_id, lacto_fraction and this new column, to a csv in your repository. This afternoon’s notebook reads it back, and so does Wednesday’s.
How many samples land in each group? Does the split change across the three visits?



Part 3: Check the agent

Ask Pi to compute the Lactobacillus fraction. Then check: does its answer for one sample you compute by hand agree to three decimal places?
A common failure is matching genus names with the wrong case or with partial matching, so that Lactobacillus also catches something it should not. Ask it which species names it matched, and read the list.
lacto_fraction must lie between 0 and 1 for every sample. Check the minimum and maximum.
Ask it to justify the 0.5 cutoff. The answer will sound confident. Decide for yourself whether the reasoning holds up.



Part 4: Reach (optional)
Build the same per-sample summary table for one of the group project datasets, group_a_probiotic or group_b_contraception. The column names are identical, so your code should run unchanged. If it does not, you hard-coded something.


Discussion

What did you filter, and what did you lose?
The 0.5 cutoff is arbitrary. What would change in your conclusions if it were 0.3, or 0.8?
We are about to use a grouping built from the species table to test the gene table. Why is that a fair thing to do, and what would make it unfair?

People are on their feet for the first forty-five minutes and at tables with pen and paper for the rest. The slides for every step are at the end of this afternoon’s deck.

Tape the floor axes in an open part of the room: one long line left to right (more blue toward the right), and one line front to back crossing it at the left end (more orange toward the back, more green toward the front).
Sort the printed cards in order, S01 first. The deck is interleaved, so handing out the first 61 cards still gives a balanced room. Keep the rest as spares.


Run sheet

Bags and balls (12 min)
Put the four bags on a table at the front and ask for eight volunteers, two per bag. Without looking, the first person at each bag draws 5 pom-poms and the second draws 20. Each tallies their colours on the back of a blank card, colours the bar on the front, and copies the bag’s inflammation tag. Hold the pairs of cards up side by side.
Ask the room:

Did the two people at the same bag make the same card?
Which of the two cards do you trust more? Why?
If the 5-ball card were all you had, what would you conclude about that bag?


Which bag you pick is biological variation, and which balls you draw is measurement variation. Every sample this week carries both, and sequencing deeper only reduces the second.



Hand out cards (3 min)
Give everyone one printed card. The eight volunteers keep their hand-made card. Explain the card on the slide: the front shows proportions, so every bar is the same length, and the small n is how many balls were drawn. The back has the counts and the inflammation tag. The printed cards came from the same kind of bags.


Round 1: closest partner, then pairs of pairs (12 min)

Everyone finds the one card most like theirs and stands together, judging by the bars and ignoring the card numbers. A group of three is fine.
Each pair finds its closest pair.
Each group of four finds its closest group.

While they move, draw the merges on the whiteboard as a tree: two names joined, then two pairs joined. That drawing is a dendrogram.
Ask the room:

How did you decide two cards were similar? That rule is a distance.
When two groups both wanted the same pair, how did you settle it? That choice is the linkage rule, and software makes it for you.
Who had trouble finding a partner? Look at the n on their card.


This is hierarchical clustering. Tomorrow afternoon the distance gets a name, Bray-Curtis, and the tree gets drawn by a computer.



Round 2: the floor is a plot (10 min)
Everyone stands where their card belongs on the taped axes: left to right by how much of the bar is blue, back to front by orange share minus green share. Take a photo from as high as you can, a chair is enough. The slides have a precomputed version of the plot if the photo does not work out.
Ask the room:

The blue and pink cards are standing close together. Are their bars alike?
We chose these two axes. What would you need to separate everyone properly?


A PCoA is the computer choosing the axes for you. It finds the directions along which the cards differ most, and it reports how much of the difference each axis captures.



Reveal and debrief (8 min)
Go past the spoiler slide. Show which bag each card came from, then the computer versions of both rounds: the floor plot, the PCoA, and the dendrogram.
Points to pull out:

Cards with 5 to 10 balls end up in the wrong place more often. Too few reads turn into ordination error.
Blends stand between groups. Real communities shift, and a clustering forces each one into a single group anyway.
Two axes squash the blue and pink bags together. A third axis separates them.



Build the table (35 min)
People sit with whoever is near them. Groups will be different sizes, and that is fine. Each person gets a worksheet, and the group pools its cards.
On side 1, everyone copies the group’s cards into the columns, one card per column. The feature metadata is printed on the sheet. Point out the layout: sample information sits above the columns it describes, feature information sits beside the rows it describes. That alignment is what R has to keep in sync.
Side 2 has the questions. Walk round and push on these:

Collapsing the rows: “makes lactic acid” plus “encodes lysin” does not equal the column total, because green is in both groups. Taxonomy is a hierarchy, so every row has one parent and adding up is safe. Gene sets overlap, so one gene counts in many sets, which matters for enrichment on Thursday.
Keeping only high inflammation: crossing out columns in the counts means crossing out the same entries in the sample metadata, and the feature metadata stays as it is.



Report to the room (5 min)
Each group copies its two-by-two table (mostly lactic acid or not, high or low inflammation) onto the flip chart with its n. Add up the columns for the room total.
Ask the room:

Did your table show the pattern the room shows?
Was any group wrong, or just small?


On Wednesday afternoon you will put a p-value on this question and see how it changes with n.



Close (5 min)
Leave the flip chart up. Tomorrow morning the table has 220 rows of bacteria or 14,226 rows of human genes, and 471 columns, and the column totals and proportions from the worksheet are the first things you compute in R.

title: Group Project
section: Session 1 — Wednesday: Build a data dossier
text:
Session 1 — Wednesday: Build a data dossier
Your group is going to build a data dossier: a Quarto report that explains your dataset table-by-table, shows what the numbers look like, and ends with a shortlist of biological questions you plan to explore more on Thursday.
Use Pi to move fast, then slow down and interrogate/iterate on what Pi produced. Pi will hand you a working draft in seconds. The learning happens when you read its code, ask it for clarification, run it, and check that it’s actually true.

Work in parallel, then compare
Everyone should try prompting Pi on their codespace. Compare often. When someone in your group got more out of the dataset than you did, ask:

“What did you ask Pi for?”



The Pi loop
Start by copying this prompt into the terminal:
I'm exploring a new dataset in `data/`. Ask me which group I'm in, then read all
the CSV files and give me, for each one, what a single row represents and
what every column means. Always make files in the "group_project" folder.

I want the output in the form of a qmd document using R and tidyverse code for each code chunk. I want 
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    embed-resources: true 
Launch the preview as a detached background process so it survives your shell
exiting and keeps watching for changes:
    PORT=4321
    setsid quarto preview <qmd_file_name> --no-browser --port $PORT \
      > /tmp/quarto-preview.log 2>&1 < /dev/null &
We're in a GitHub Codespace, so localhost won't work from my browser. Build the
forwarded URL from the Codespace env vars and print it as a clickable terminal
hyperlink (short visible text, so it won't wrap and break the link):
    URL="https://${CODESPACE_NAME}-${PORT}.${GITHUB_CODESPACES_PORT_FORWARDING_DOMAIN}/"
    printf '\n\e]8;;%s\a▶ Open Quarto preview\e]8;;\a\n' "$URL"
    echo "log: /tmp/quarto-preview.log"
This might take 2-5+ minutes for the model to accomplish. Then start these steps below:

Ask. Give Pi a concrete task. (for instance “Tell me what the second code chunk does, line by line”)
Read. Actually read the code and the response it wrote. What does each line do? If a line is mysterious, ask Pi to explain that line.
Verify. Don’t just trust it; it’s still your job to produce trustworthy analysis. Check it two ways: by doing (run a little of your own code to count the rows, count() a column’s values, or confirm a join lines up) and by asking (have Pi tell you how it would verify the claim, then run what it suggests).
Iterate. Refine, then write one sentence in your report saying what you now know.

Pi might be completely right, and that’s fine. You verify anyway, because the goal is for you to understand the dataset.


Your report
One rendered HTML report per group. Start your .qmd with a header that turns on a table of contents, folds code by default, and bundles everything into a single self-contained file:
---
title: "Group A — Data Dossier"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
    embed-resources: true
---
code-fold keeps the report readable as prose while leaving every chunk one click away; embed-resources makes the HTML a single file you can hand to anyone.


The afternoon (1:30–5:00)

1:30–1:45 · Kick off & set up. Each person creates their report .qmd with the header above, loads tidyverse and here, and confirms the data path works. Goal: a Quarto doc that renders before you explore anything.
1:45–2:45 · Map the dataset, fast. Lean on Pi for speed. For every table, answer: what is one row, and what does each column mean? Get a rough draft of the whole map written as prose in your report.
2:45–3:00 · First verification. Slow down. Each person picks two claims from their map and confirms them — by running your own code and by asking Pi how it would check. Not hunting for mistakes; building confidence that you really know what’s in the tables.
3:00–3:30 · Break.
3:30–4:30 · Explore & plot. Go deep on the numbers: distributions, skew, suspicious values, missing data. Make your first plots inside the report and iterate on them — remaking one plot three times teaches more than making three different plots once.
4:30–5:00 · Distill & render. Pool everyone’s findings into the group report. Turn what you found into a shortlist of biological questions for Thursday. Render to HTML.



Walk away with

A rendered data dossier that explains every table and shows a few plots
A shortlist of 2–4 candidate questions for Thursday
A sense of which of you asks Pi the sharpest questions, and why

title: Group Project
section: Session 2 — Thursday: Table 1, comparisons, and models
text:
Session 2 — Thursday: Table 1, comparisons, and models
Wednesday’s dossier told you what is in the dataset. Thursday you take one of your candidate questions and answer it three ways: describe the participants, compare the groups, and fit a model. The output this time is the analysis a paper would actually show.
You keep working with Pi in the same loop as Wednesday — ask, read, verify, iterate — adding to the report you already have.

The three pieces
Build these for the question your group picked. You don’t have to use all three; pick the ones your question needs, and be ready Friday to say why.

A Table 1 with gtsummary. tbl_summary(by = <group>) describes your participants and add_p() tests each row. Go variable by variable and decide whether the default summary (median (IQR), counts (%)) and the default test are the ones you want, then override the ones that aren’t.
A comparison figure with ggpubr. ggboxplot(...) + stat_compare_means() shows one outcome across your groups with the p-value drawn on the plot. Reach for facet_wrap() when you want to screen several outcomes at once.
A model with tbl_regression(). Fit lm(), glm(), or lmer() for the effect you care about — adjusting for a covariate, or accounting for repeated samples on the same participant — then turn the fit into a coefficient table. Fit the model once and report it; never refit just to make a table.



Add to the report you already have
Your dossier .qmd from Wednesday is the right place for all of this. Your preview may still be running; if not, relaunch it the same way you did in Session 1. When Pi edits the file and saves, the preview reloads on its own, so keep it visible next to the terminal and watch each change land.
Ask Pi to add to the file, and point it at the section you mean:
In group_project/<your_report>.qmd, add a new section called "Table 1".
Use gtsummary to build a tbl_summary of the participant metadata split by
<group>, then pipe to add_p() to test each row. Append it to the file —
don't rewrite what's already there. I'll watch the preview reload.
Then iterate one change at a time, reading the preview after each:
Age should be mean (SD) with a t-test, not median (IQR). Override just that
one row and leave the rest of the table alone.
Now add a ggpubr boxplot of <outcome> by <group> with a Wilcoxon p-value on
it, right below the table.
The first version is rarely the one you want: the wrong test, the wrong grouping, ugly labels. That is normal. Fix one thing, watch the preview, read what changed, and decide whether it is better. That loop is the work.


Verify, same as Wednesday
A model fit and a p-value look authoritative whether or not they are right. Before a result goes in your Friday talk, check it. Does the test match the data (skewed data wants Wilcoxon, symmetric wants a t-test)? Does the figure’s p-value agree with the table’s? Ask Pi how it would confirm the result, then run that check yourself.


The afternoon (1:30–5:00)

1:30–1:45 · Pick the question. As a group, settle on one question from Wednesday’s shortlist and the groups you will compare. Write it at the top of the section you’re about to build.
1:45–2:45 · Table 1. Build tbl_summary() |> add_p(), then go column by column deciding which defaults to keep and which to override. Land on one Table 1 the group agrees on.
2:45–3:00 · Sanity check. Confirm the test choices match the distributions you saw on Wednesday.
3:00–3:30 · Break.
3:30–4:30 · Compare and model. Add the ggpubr figure(s) for your headline comparison, then fit the model that answers your question and report it with tbl_regression(). Iterate on the plot — remaking one figure three times beats making three different ones once.
4:30–5:00 · Distill & render. Decide which table and which figure tell your story, write the sentence or two that goes with each, and render to HTML.



Walk away with

A Table 1 you would feel OK putting in a paper
One or two ggpubr figures of the comparisons you care about
At least one model reported with tbl_regression()
A clear sense of what your group will say on Friday

Full prompts live in group_project/README_session2.md in your codespace.

Three questions

Does inflammation (IL-1a) rise during menstruation?
Does the neutrophil share of immune cells change across the cycle?
Does birth control shift the cytokine milieu?

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The question
Bleeding is a tissue-remodelling event, so we expect inflammation to track it.
Does IL-1a rise during menstruation and settle afterwards? Each woman is measured four times, so we fit a model with a per-participant random effect and let the week-before-bleeding be the reference point.

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The code
il1 <- cyt |> filter(cytokine == "IL-1a")

fit <- lmer(log(conc) ~ time_point + (1 | pid), data = il1)

tbl_regression(fit, intercept = TRUE)
time_point is a factor ordered from the week before bleeding, so every coefficient reads as a change relative to that baseline week. (1 | pid) accounts for the four correlated samples per woman.

Abbreviation: CI = Confidence Interval

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
What it means
On the log scale, relative to the week before bleeding:

Onset: +2.3 — roughly a tenfold jump in IL-1a (p < 0.001).
End of bleeding: +2.0 — still strongly elevated.
Week after: +0.3 — back to baseline (p = 0.4).

Inflammation rises sharply with bleeding and resolves within a week. The cytokine milieu is a moving target that depends entirely on when in the cycle you sample — a key lesson for designing studies like this one.

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The question
The Part 1 overview hinted that neutrophils’ share of immune cells changes during bleeding. Let’s test it properly.
The outcome is a proportion of counted cells, so the natural model is binomial — exactly the flow-cytometry recipe from the modeling lecture. Because the cell counts are huge, a plain binomial is wildly overconfident, so we add a per-sample random effect to capture the real sample-to-sample spread.

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The code
flow <- flow |> mutate(other = cd45_positive - neutrophils)

fit <- glmer(
  cbind(neutrophils, other) ~ time_point + (1 | pid) + (1 | sample_id),
  family = binomial(), data = flow
)

# the figure: observed neutrophil share across the cycle
ggboxplot(flow, x = "time_point", y = "prop_neut",
          fill = "time_point", palette = "Set1") +
  stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", ref.group = "week_prior",
                     label = "p.signif")

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The question
Hormonal contraception changes the cervicovaginal environment, so we might expect it to leave a cytokine signature.
Does any cytokine differ between the birth-control and no-birth-control arms? We screen the well-detected cytokines and correct for multiple testing.

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The code
keep <- c("IL-1a", "IP-10", "MIP-3a", "MIG")   # detected in >75% of samples

panel <- cyt |> filter(limits == "not_censored", cytokine %in% keep)

ggboxplot(panel, x = "arm", y = "conc", fill = "arm",
          palette = "Set1", facet.by = "cytokine") +
  scale_y_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.2))) +
  stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", label = "p.format")

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
What we found

Inflammation rises and falls with bleeding — IL-1a jumps ~10x at onset and resets within a week.
Neutrophils’ share of immune cells dips during bleeding, then rebounds.
Birth control left no detectable cytokine signature against that much larger cyclic signal.

title: The vaginal immune environment across the menstrual cycle
text:
The takeaway
Timing dominates. Any study of the vaginal immune environment has to account for cycle stage before it can ask about anything else.

Exercise 1: Demographics and Table 1

Part 1 — Predict (no code)
For each non-pid column of table_01 (arm, smoker, age, education, sex), predict — in plain words, before running anything:

How will tbl_summary(by = arm) summarise it? Mean (SD)? Median (IQR)? Counts (%)?
Is the column skewed or symmetric, sparse or dense? That same judgment is what decides which test add_p() reaches for.



Part 2 — Build

text:
Exercise 2: Figures with p-values

Mode flip. If you were agentic in Exercise 1, you are manual now; if you were manual, you are agentic. Same definitions as before — manual means you may ask a chat LLM conceptual questions but it does not touch your notebook.

Open notebooks/06-figures-with-pvalues.qmd in your Codespace.

Part 1 — Read three plots (no code)
The notebook shows three pre-built plots: the single-outcome ggboxplot (pH by arm at week 7), the six-cytokine facet_wrap panel, and the paired pre-post line plot. For each plot:

What is the mark?
What is the comparison being tested?
What test is on it, and how do you know?
How many rows of data made each mark?



Part 2 — Build
Build the four analyses, growing toward a publication-ready set.

ggboxplot(table_02 |> filter(time_point == "week_7"), x = "arm", y = "ph", fill = "arm") + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test"). The visual form of Table 2 row “ph”.
Build the same plot in plain ggplot: ggplot(...) + geom_boxplot() + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test"). Confirm both give the same p-value.
The cytokine panel: filter table_03 to six chosen cytokines and limits == "within limits", join table_00 to attach arm and time_point, filter to week_7, then ggplot + geom_boxplot + facet_wrap(~ cytokine, scales = "free_y") + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test").
The paired pre-post: filter table_02 to baseline and week_7, mutate(time_point = fct_relevel(time_point, "baseline", "week_7")), then ggplot + geom_line(aes(group = pid)) + geom_point + facet_wrap(~ arm) + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", paired = TRUE, comparisons = list(c("baseline", "week_7"))).
The adjusted analysis: join table_01 onto a week_7 slice of table_02, fit lm(ph ~ arm + age + smoker), pipe to tbl_regression().



Part 3 — Reach (optional)
Pick one of the four analyses and polish it for publication (axis labels, theme, panel ordering, p-value formatting, color palette).
Or, repeat the full analysis arc on nugent_score or crp_blood instead of ph. The pattern is identical; only the column name changes.


Discussion
Once the room is back together: pick one result from the five analyses you built that you would be willing to put in a paper. What is the test behind it, and how would you defend that choice to a skeptical reviewer?

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Learning Outcomes

Explain models as a description of how we think the data were generated, and distinguish between the associated “large” and “small” worlds.
Differentiate between the members of the biostatistical model zoo and explain the types of outcomes and questions to which they are well-suited.
Use R to implement these models, using formula syntax to specify the relationship between covariates and outcomes, and interpret the estimated model parameters in the original problem context.
Diagnose model limitations using visualization and simulation.
Describe how to improve model fit by modifying assumptions (adding covariates, random effects, interactions).

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Part 1: What is a Model?

Below are a few views of IL-1a concentration from the workshop dataset. Notice the variation across people and a possible treatment effect at the post-treatment visit.

ids <- read_csv(here("datasets/instructional_dataset/00_sample_ids_UKZN_workshop_2023.csv"))
il1 <- read_csv(here("datasets/instructional_dataset/03_elisa_cytokines_UKZN_workshop_2023.csv")) |>
 filter(cytokine == "IL-1a") |>
 left_join(ids)
head(il1)

p1 <- ggplot(il1) +
 geom_line(aes(time_point, log(conc), group = pid, col = arm)) +
 scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
 scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0))

p2 <- ggplot(il1) +
 geom_histogram(aes(log(conc), fill = arm), bins = 10, position = "identity", alpha = 0.6) +
 facet_wrap(~ time_point)

(p1 / p2) +
 plot_layout(guides = "collect")








Imagine running the study again, keeping the recruitment and experimental protocols as similar as possible. Make two lists,

Aspects of these plots that you think will continue to be true in the new experiment.
Aspects of these plots that you think will be different.

Take 5 minutes to prepare your description.
A statistical model is a simplified description of how we think the data were generated (the “data story”).
Large vs. small worlds. We should distinguish the “large world” where the data were gathered from the “small world” of the statistical model. The small world makes its assumptions precise, allows hypothetical interventions, and quantifies uncertainty. But there will always be a gap between the two worlds, and that is itself a source of uncertainty not captured by the model.
Modeling Checklist. Organize the work of modeling into these steps.

Biological Question. A good model should clarify our thinking about a real phenomenon and not be made just for the sake of modeling.
Plot the Data. What does the outcome look like? Do you already notice any relationships with other variables?
Working Assumptions. Make a small-world story for how the data were generated. This is the initial statistical model.
Model Checks. Use simulation and diagnostics to check whether the model captures patterns we see in the real data.
Revised Models. Revise the working assumptions until the model provides a good match. This model can now be used to answer the original biological question.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
section: Part 2: A Tour through the Model Zoo
text:
Part 2: A Tour through the Model Zoo
Each type of statistical model is designed for a different kind of data or biological question. Knowing all the “species” of model will let you adapt to whatever data or questions you encounter.

Bernoulli and Binomial Models

Bernoulli and binomial models apply when outcomes fall into two groups. The Bernoulli models individual outcomes while the binomial applies to their totals.

Infected vs. not infected
Responder vs. non-responder
Alive vs. dead

A Bernoulli model can simulate new data with frequencies of blue and orange circles similar to (but not exactly the same as) those we originally observed.

A Bernoulli model expects each sample to be associated with a 0/1 label, while the binomial models counts of each group.

The data generating mechanism can let the frequency depend on sample characteristics, e.g., large circles are more likely to be blue.

The model can learn the relationship between the size covariates and probability of the blue outcome and summarizes it as a smooth, increasing curve.

Imagine modeling a disease outbreak in a county. Each person can be infected or not. The probability of infection can depend on the degree of social interaction. This data story is analogous to the large-size and blue circles data story.

infections <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/infections.csv") |>
 mutate(infected = ifelse(infected == "infected", 1, 0))


infections

# A tibble: 100 × 5
   sample_id social_contact county    prob_infection infected
   <chr>              <dbl> <chr>              <dbl>    <dbl>
 1 sample_1          0.748  county_4           0.561        1
 2 sample_2          0.379  county_6           0.297        0
 3 sample_3          0.483  county_2           0.366        0
 4 sample_4          0.813  county_2           0.608        0

 9 sample_9          0.935  county_2           0.691        0
10 sample_10         0.849  county_5           0.634        1
# ℹ 90 more rows



ggplot(infections) +
 geom_jitter(aes(social_contact, infected, col = factor(infected)), height = 0.05) +
 geom_line(aes(social_contact, prob_infection), linewidth = 1, col = "#232323") +
 scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
 labs(
     y = "Probability of Infection",
     x = "Level of Social Contact",
     col = "Infection Status"
 )








The binomial model applies when we see totals within categories, but not person-level outcomes.

infections_props <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/infections_props.csv")


infections_props

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  social_level   not_infected infected total
  <chr>                 <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 (0.0129,0.337]           29        6    35
2 (0.337,0.661]            20        9    29
3 (0.661,0.985]            17       19    36



infections_props |>
 select(-total) |>
 pivot_longer(-social_level) |>
 ggplot() +
 geom_col(aes(social_level, value, fill = name), position = "dodge") +
 scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0.1, 0)) +
 labs(
     x = "Level of Social Contact",
     y = "Count",
     fill = "Infection Status"
 )








To fit these models, we can use the glm function. This function has three arguments,

formula: A formula like y ~ x specifies the relationship between the model outcome y and contextual variables x, which we will call “covariates.”
family: The type of model to use for the given dataset. This depends on the data type for the outcome (binary, count, etc.) and it differs across the examples in this section.
data: A data.frame object whose columns give the response and predictor variables to use in the model. Any terms appearing in the formula must be column names in this data.frame.

For example, for a Bernoulli model to have probability of infection depend on social_contact, we can use the command below. Even though we set family = binomial(), the fact that infected is a 0/1 variable means that internally the command uses a Bernoulli model1.

fit <- glm(infected ~ social_contact, family = binomial(), data = infections)
summary(fit)


Call:
glm(formula = infected ~ social_contact, family = binomial(), 
    data = infections)

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)     -2.3702     0.5739  -4.130 3.63e-05 ***
social_contact   3.0933     0.8908   3.473 0.000515 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 128.21  on 99  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 113.69  on 98  degrees of freedom
AIC: 117.69

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4


The Estimate column describes how infection probability changes across levels of social contact. As given, they are not easily interpretable2. The plogis function converts them to the probability scale. The (Intercept) estimate sets the predicted probability at zero social contact, while the social_contact estimate sets how steeply that probability increases with social contact.



plogis(-2.37) # when social contact = 0

[1] 0.08548914

plogis(-2.37 + 0.5 * 3.09) # when social contact = 0.5

[1] 0.3047033

plogis(-2.37 + 1 * 3.09) # when social contact = 1

[1] 0.672607


This Bernoulli model is often called logistic regression, after the inverse logistic function (plogis) that converts model estimates to the probability scale.
The infection data were simulated with a true social_contact effect of 3. The estimate 3.09 is close, but even with 100 samples, slightly off. Nonetheless, it lies within one standard error (0.89) of the truth – the model gives both an estimate of the effect and a measure of its uncertainty.

infections$predicted_prob <- plogis(predict(fit))
ggplot(infections) +
 geom_jitter(aes(social_contact, infected, col = factor(infected)), height = 0.05) +
 geom_line(aes(social_contact, prob_infection), linewidth = 1, col = "#bbb6b6") +
 geom_line(aes(social_contact, predicted_prob), linewidth = 1, col = "#414ca1") +
 scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
 labs(
     y = "Probability of Infection",
     x = "Level of Social Contact",
     col = "Infection Status",
     title = "Original (gray) vs. fitted (blue) infection probability"
 )








The same function fits the binomial model, but the formula’s left-hand side needs to account for group-level counts, not person-level outcomes. Also, the weights argument is added to reflect the different totals in each category.

fit <- glm(infected / total  ~ social_level, family = binomial(), weights = total, data = infections_props)
summary(fit)


Call:
glm(formula = infected/total ~ social_level, family = binomial(), 
    data = infections_props, weights = total)

Coefficients:
                          Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                -1.5755     0.4485  -3.513 0.000443 ***
social_level(0.337,0.661]   0.7770     0.6019   1.291 0.196703    
social_level(0.661,0.985]   1.6868     0.5591   3.017 0.002554 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance:  1.0418e+01  on 2  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: -9.5479e-15  on 0  degrees of freedom
AIC: 17.201

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 3


plogis converts these estimates to the probability scale. The low category is absorbed into the intercept. For the other two, add their coefficient to the intercept before converting to probabilities for that category.




Poisson and Negative Binomial Models

Poisson and negative binomial models apply to count data. The Poisson arises whenever we count events spread uniformly across space and time, for example, the number of raindrops landing on a window during a minute of rain.

Making a histogram of these counts over time gives us a simple data story. We get a random number of raindrops each minute. Most of the time around five drops land, but a value of zero or ten would not be unusual. Values much larger than that are less likely.

Many biological counts have this flavor.

Transcripts counts in a cell
Mutation count along a segment of the genome
Infection count within a county

Exercise: The last example is again about infections, which we saw in the Bernoulli and binomial examples. What did we know there we don’t know from infection counts alone?
In the data story, we can allow the typical count to depend on sample characteristics. For example, the rain may have been most intense earlier in the night. This figure shows how the probabilities of different number of raindrops progress.

For a more realistic example, note that the infections in counties closer to the epicenter likely have more infections.

Residual deviance: 108.18  on 98  degrees of freedom
AIC: 304.64

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 5


The model output is reported on a log scale, so it should be interpreted after exponentiation. The fitted mean at distance 0 is exp(2.5) = 12.8, matching the plot. Similarly, larger distances are interpreted after plugging into a linear formula and exponentiating. For example, at distance 0.5, the mean is exp(2.5 - .5 * 4.3) = 1.4.

outbreak$predicted_mean <- predict(fit, type = "response")
ggplot(outbreak, aes(epicenter_distance)) +
 geom_point(aes(y = infected)) +
 geom_line(aes(y = mean), col = "#bbb6b6", linewidth = 1) +
 geom_line(aes(y = predicted_mean), col = "#414ca1", linewidth = 1) +
 labs(
     x = "Epicenter Distance",
     y = "Infection Count",
     title = "Original (gray) vs. fitted (blue) mean count"
 )








Exercise: What is the level of uncertainty in these estimates? How would you interpret 0.08 in the S.E. column? What about 0.29?
Often unmeasured factors influence the rates, making the data more heterogeneous than the Poisson can handle. For example, infection might depend on not only distance to the epicenter but also unknown, county-specific population densities. The negative binomial distribution addresses this – it arises as a mixture of Poissons with similar but slightly different rates. In the data simulated below, the counts at a given distance are more spread out even though the blue mean line is unchanged.

outbreak_nb <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/outbreak_nb.csv")


head(outbreak_nb)

5 sample5                0.611 1.06  county_5        0
6 sample6                0.473 1.83  county_6        6

 geom_point(aes(y = infected)) +
 labs(
     x = "Epicenter Distance",
     y = "Infection Count"
 )








glm doesn’t provide a negative binomial model, but glm.nb from the MASS package does, with the same syntax as glm.

fit <- glm.nb(infected ~ epicenter_distance, data = outbreak_nb)
summary(fit)


Call:
glm.nb(formula = infected ~ epicenter_distance, data = outbreak_nb, 
    init.theta = 1.888724811, link = log)

Linear Regression Models

When the response is continuous, linear regression applies. For example, it can be used for,

Antibody titre
CRP concentration

The model assumes symmetric, random error around a mean value that depends on the inputs. For example, antibody titre might vary as a linear function of age.

antibody <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/antibody.csv")


head(antibody)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  sample_id   age blood_pressure  mean antibody
  <chr>     <dbl>          <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
1 sample_1   31.9           99.5  21.6     22.7
2 sample_2   78.2          113.   23.9     27.5
3 sample_3   25.0          118.   21.3     20.2
4 sample_4   31.5           71.0  21.6     17.6
5 sample_5   21.4          120.   21.1     20.3
6 sample_6   45.2          131.   22.3     22.4



ggplot(antibody) +
 geom_line(aes(age, mean), col = "#d53636", linewidth = 1.5) +
 geom_point(aes(age, antibody)) +
 labs(x = "Age", y = "Antibody Titre")








Underlying these observations is a linear function with random Gaussian errors.

The lm function fits this model, with the same inputs as glm, but no family. The estimates give predicted values at age \(x\) \(19.6 + 0.058 x\). For example, at age 10, the prediction is \(19.6 + 0.58 \approx 20.18\).

fit <- lm(antibody ~ age, antibody)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = antibody ~ age, data = antibody)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-5.345 -1.076 -0.076  1.325  6.698 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)

Residual standard error: 2.205 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2428, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2351 
F-statistic: 31.42 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 1.911e-07


What makes Gaussian errors a reasonable assumption? This distribution appears across statistics because of the central limit theorem: the average of many small independent effects tends to a Gaussian distribution. You can find a nice animation of this result here. In this example, we’re implicitly assuming many small, independent factors besides age that perturb the observed antibody measurement.




Survival Models

Survival models describe whether and when an event occurs. For example,

Time until heart attack
Time until loan default
Time until HIV acquisition

If the event doesn’t occur over the study or if they drop out, the participant’s response is called “censored.”
Unlike the other models, whose outcome is a single number, the survival outcome has two parts.

The time the event was observed. Or, if the event was never observed, the time the study ended.
Whether the event occurred (status = 1) or not (status = 0) before the study end.

For example, imagine modeling HIV acquisition over drug treatments, tracking participants for two years. Some have an event during the study period (status = 1, triangles) while the rest are censored.

surv_data <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/surv_data.csv")


head(surv_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  treatment hazard  time status
  <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>
1 drug       0.202 2          0
2 control    0.449 0.152      1
3 drug       0.202 0.386      1
4 control    0.449 0.629      1
5 drug       0.202 0.105      1
6 control    0.449 0.996      1



surv_data |>
 mutate(id = row_number()) |>
 ggplot(aes(time, reorder(id, time), color = treatment, shape = factor(status))) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  labs(
    x = "Time",
    y = "Participant",
    color = "Treatment",
    shape = "Event?"
  ) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_line(linewidth = 0.1))








The most popular form of survival model is the Cox proportional hazards model. During any time interval, anyone who hasn’t yet had an event is at risk for it. Some covariates can change the relative risk (“hazard”) of the event. Because a covariate shifts the hazard by the same factor at all times, the model is called a proportional hazards model.

fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ treatment, data = surv_data)
summary(fit)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ treatment, data = surv_data)

  n= 50, number of events= 31

The model output shows how each covariate rescales the hazard.
Exercise: Can you think of an example where the proportional hazards assumption does not hold? Hint: What if a drug was not effective immediately after treatment start but required several weeks to reach its full effect?



Variations: Multiple Predictors, Mixed Effects, and Interactions

Multiple Predictors. The examples above had a single covariate. We can add more covariates with + variable on the right-hand side of the formula. Each variable’s estimate is the effect of that variable with all others held fixed.
For example, if we wanted to model antibody titre as a function of both age and blood pressure, we could use the formula antibody ~ age + blood_pressure. The interpretation of the estimate below is that, fixing blood pressure level, the average antibody level increases by 0.058 units for every year increase in age.

fit <- lm(antibody ~ age + blood_pressure, data = antibody)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = antibody ~ age + blood_pressure, data = antibody)

Residuals:
   Min     1Q Median     3Q    Max 
-5.014 -1.044 -0.175  1.288  6.525 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    21.10179    1.10078  19.170  < 2e-16 ***
age             0.05839    0.01033   5.650 1.61e-07 ***
blood_pressure -0.01553    0.01003  -1.549    0.125    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.19 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2611, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2458 
F-statistic: 17.14 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: 4.239e-07



The surface can be visualized in 2D by associating each slice in 3D with a curve.

Mixed Effects. One common situation is that baseline effects (overall probabilities in Bernoulli model, rates in the Poisson, intercepts in the linear regression, …) vary across contexts. For example, infection probability might always increase with social contact, but the baseline rate may vary from county to county, due to unmeasured factors like population density and mobility.

mixed_effect_data <- read_csv("https://huggingface.co/datasets/krisrs1128/durban_workshop_data/resolve/main/mixed_effect_data.csv") |>
 mutate(infected = ifelse(infected == "infected", 1, 0))


head(mixed_effect_data)

# A tibble: 6 × 5
  social_contact county    county_re prob_infection infected
           <dbl> <chr>         <dbl>          <dbl>    <dbl>
1          0.536 county_4      0.774          0.595        0
2          0.532 county_4      0.774          0.591        1
3          0.854 county_6     -0.358          0.551        1
4          0.127 county_10     0.834          0.313        0
5          0.316 county_2     -0.482          0.177        0
6          0.346 county_8      0.212          0.321        0



ggplot(mixed_effect_data) +
 geom_jitter(aes(social_contact, infected, col = factor(infected)), height = 0.05) +
 geom_line(aes(social_contact, prob_infection), linewidth = 1, col = "#232323") +
 facet_wrap(~ reorder(county, prob_infection), nrow = 2) +
 scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
 scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
 labs(y = "Probability of Infection")








One solution is to include county as an ordinary covariate. But with many counties this becomes unwieldy – we would have a separate estimate for each. A better approach is to use a random effect (also called a hierarchical model), where the county-level effects are imagined to be drawn from a larger source of randomness. Rather than estimate each county’s effect separately, we estimate the overall variation across counties. Statistically, this is an easier task, and it yields higher power. Because they include both fixed and random effects, these models are called mixed effects models.

To implement this, we replace glm with glmer and add (1 | county) to the formula, indicating that county is a random rather than fixed effect.

fit <- glmer(infected ~ social_contact + (1 | county), family = binomial(), data = mixed_effect_data)
summary(fit)
