title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Goals for this session


Distinguish between the “large” and “small” worlds of modeling.
Compare biostatistical models and explain when they apply.
Use R to estimate models and know how to explain the output.
Diagnose and address model failures.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Let’s start with a picture

The plots below show IL-1a concentration from our workshop luminex dataset.
Notice the variation across people and a possible treatment effect at the post-treatment visit.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Discussion
Imagine running the study again, keeping the recruitment and experimental protocols as similar as possible. Make two lists:

Aspects of the plots that you think will still be true in the new experiment.
Aspects of the plots that you think will change.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
A statistical model

A statistical model is a simplified description of how the data were generated, the “data story.”


Model parameters let us answer scientific questions, like how a treatment affects outcomes.
We observe just one realization of the data generating process – things could have turned out differently if we ran the study again.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Large vs. small worlds


Large world

Where the data were actually gathered
Complex, influenced by factors we never observed
Hard to carry out controlled interventions


Small world

Inside the statistical model
Logically consistent with precisely stated assumptions
Allows hypothetical interventions and quantifies uncertainty


There will always be a gap between the two worlds. That gap is itself a source of uncertainty not captured by the model.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Large Worlds
A dataset is like a photograph of a biological system, but it develops slowly and is more error prone.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Large Worlds
A dataset is like a photograph of a biological system, but the snapshot takes longer to generate and is more error prone.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Large Worlds
A dataset is like a photograph of a biological system, but the snapshot takes longer to generate and is more error prone.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Small Worlds

The small-world model summarizes what would stay true if the experiment were repeated.
It encodes a data generating process that lets us simulate new data with the experiment’s key features, without memorizing every sample.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Modeling Checklist


Biological Question. What real-world questions do you want to answer?
Plot the Data. What does the outcome look like? Do you notice relationships with other variables?
Working Assumptions. Make a small-world story for how the data were generated. This is the initial statistical model.
Model Checks. Use simulation and diagnostics to check whether the model captures patterns we see in the real data.
Revised Models. Revise until the model provides a good match. Use this to answer the original question.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Recipes
Each type of statistical model is designed for a different kind of data or biological question.
Like having a well-stocked pantry is needed to cook many recipes, knowing the basic statistical ingredients will allow you to adapt to whatever data or questions you encounter.

Today’s tour:

Bernoulli — binary outcomes
Poisson — count outcomes
Linear regression — continuous outcomes
Variations — multiple predictors, mixed effects, interactions

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Models
These models apply when outcomes fall into two groups.

Heads vs. tails
Infected vs. not infected
Responder vs. non-responder
CD3- cell vs. not CD3- cell


The Bernoulli is for individual outcomes, the Binomial applies to their totals

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Models
The raw data come from two classes, and we want their relative probabilities.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Models
The raw data come from two classes, and we want their relative probabilities.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Model Covariates
The outcome probabilities can depend on sample-level covariates.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Small World Model
Data Story: More social contact → higher probability of infection.

Response \(y\): Who does (1) or doesn’t (0) get infected during an outbreak?
Covariates \(x\): Some people have larger social networks than others.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Fitting with glm
The glm function has three arguments:

formula: written y ~ x, this relates outcome y to covariates x
family: the type of model (depends on the data type of the outcome)
data: a data.frame containing the columns named in formula

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Bernoulli fit

fit <- glm(infected ~ social_contact, family = binomial(), data = infections)
summary(fit)


Call:
glm(formula = infected ~ social_contact, family = binomial(), 
    data = infections)

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)     -2.3702     0.5739  -4.130 3.63e-05 ***
social_contact   3.0933     0.8908   3.473 0.000515 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 128.21  on 99  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 113.69  on 98  degrees of freedom
AIC: 117.69

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4



We wrote family = binomial(), but since infected is 0/1, the code knows to run a Bernoulli model.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Interpreting the fit

The estimates are on the log-odds scale, which isn’t directly interpretable.
plogis() converts them to the probability scale:
This model is often called logistic regression, after the inverse logistic function (plogis).

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Interpreting the fit
At social contact level x, the infection probability ≈ plogis(-2.37 + 3.09x)

x = 0 \(\implies\) plogis(-2.37) ≈ 0.085
x = 0.5 \(\implies\) plogis(-2.37 + 3.09 * 0.5) ≈ 0.24
x = 1 \(\implies\) plogis(-2.37 + 3.09 * 1) ≈ 0.50


summary(fit)

    data = infections)

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Interpreting the fit

The intercept parameter controls the height of the curve at 0.
The slope parameter controls the rate of its increase as a function of \(x\).

title: Modeling and Uncertainty

x = 0 \(\implies\) plogis(-2.37) ≈ 0.085

x = 1 \(\implies\) plogis(-2.37 + 3.09 * 1) ≈ 0.67

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Poisson Models
These models apply to count data.
The Poisson arises as the “number of occurrences of an event that happens rarely but has many opportunities to happen” (1). The number of raindrops landing on a small window during a heavy storm would be Poisson distributed.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Poisson Models
These models apply to count data.
The Poisson arises as the “number of occurrences of an event that happens rarely but has many opportunities to happen” (1). The number of raindrops landing on a small window during a heavy storm would be Poisson distributed.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Poisson Models
Counts can depend on sample characteristics. The rain may have been falling harder earlier in the night.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Poisson Models
Many biological counts have this flavor:

Transcript counts

Many transcripts, each with small chance of binding to cDNA
The number of transcripts of a gene might depend on drug treatment

Mutation count along a genome segment

Many base pairs with small chance of being mutated
The number of mutations depends on selection pressure

Infection count within a county

Many people with small probability of being infected
The infection rates decrease further from the epicenter

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Outbreak counts vs. distance
Let’s fit a model for the infection count example.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Outbreak counts vs. distance
Counts can depend on sample characteristics, like more infections in counties closer to the outbreak epicenter.



Table 2


outbreak |>
    select(sample_id, epicenter_distance, infected)

# A tibble: 100 × 3

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Why Gaussian errors?
The Central Limit Theorem: the average of many small, independent effects tends toward a Gaussian distribution.
We implicitly assume many small, independent factors other than age that perturb the observed antibody measurement.

Discussion

Study participants have been grouped into low and high inflammation groups. We want to see whether abundance of a given microbe-produced metabolite is associated with inflammation group.
Study participants have been grouped into HIV-free and HIV-positive groups. We want to see whether HIV status is related to proportion of Lactobacillus in the vaginal microbiome.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Mixed effects

Baseline effects often vary across contexts.
In the Bernoulli example, the way infection probability increases with social contact may vary across counties due to unmeasured factors, like population density.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text: County-varying baselines

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Random effects

We could add county as an ordinary covariate — but with many counties, this becomes unwieldy.
A better approach is to use a random effect
We imagine county effects as draws from a shared distribution.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Random effects

We estimate the overall variation across counties, not each one separately.
This is statistically easier, so it yields higher power.
Because they include both fixed and random effects, these are called mixed effects models.

text:

Replace glm with glmer and add (1 | county) to the formula.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Variations recap

Although we introduced these with Bernoulli and linear regression examples, they apply to any of the models we’ve seen.
They are the key tools we can use when revising a model’s working assumptions to improve its fit.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Discussion
Think through the first three parts of the modeling checklist for a dataset that you are interested in from your own work or study.

Biological Question. What real-world questions do you want to answer?
Plot the Data. Did you ever plot the data? If so, what patterns did you see? If not, what plots could you make?
Working Assumptions. Make a small-world story about your data. What model type, response \(y\), and covariates \(x\) could you use?

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Case Study: Longitudinal Cytokines
Biological Question

Does treatment with the anti-inflammatory drug change cytokine concentrations post-treatment (week 1), and if so does the effect persist into the long run (week 7)?

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Plot the data

There seems to be a strong treatment effect at one week that weakens by week 7. We’ll focus on IL-1a, the cytokine with the fewest measurements below the detection limit.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Working assumptions

Luminex gives a continuous readout → linear regression
Many small, unrelated factors perturb the measurement → Gaussian error
Errors are likely multiplicative, not additive → model log-concentration

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
A first model

cytokines <- cytokines |> filter(cytokine == "IL-1a")
fit <- lm(log(conc) ~ arm, data = cytokines)
summary(fit)

Check by simulation

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
What went wrong?

✅ Overall concentrations are in the correct range
✅ Control group has larger concentrations than treatment
❌ In the real data, most blue curves decrease at week 1
❌ In the simulation, about half the curves increase

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Revising the model

We gave the model no temporal information. We could fix this with the formula: log(conc) ~ arm + time_point.

This data story isn’t reasonable either
We don’t expect IL-1a concentration to change just because the clock reads week 1 or 7.


We want the treatment effect itself to depend on the week, a type of interaction: log(conc) ~ arm + arm : time_point.

title: Modeling and Uncertainty
text:
Mixed-effects version
The model treats each sample as independent, but measurements from the same participant are dependent.

Dependence reduces the effective sample size.
We can add a participant-level random effect to introduce dependence.


fit <- lmer(log(conc) ~ arm + arm : time_point + (1 | pid), data = cytokines)

Interpretation

Visually, the model doesn’t seem much better.

Build the four analyses, growing toward a publication-ready set.

ggboxplot(table_02 |> filter(time_point == "week_7"), x = "arm", y = "ph", fill = "arm") + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test"). The visual form of Table 2 row “ph”.

The cytokine panel: filter table_03 to six chosen cytokines and limits == "within limits", join table_00 to attach arm and time_point, filter to week_7, then ggplot + geom_boxplot + facet_wrap(~ cytokine, scales = "free_y") + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test").
The paired pre-post: filter table_02 to baseline and week_7, mutate(time_point = fct_relevel(time_point, "baseline", "week_7")), then ggplot + geom_line(aes(group = pid)) + geom_point + facet_wrap(~ arm) + stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", paired = TRUE, comparisons = list(c("baseline", "week_7"))).
The adjusted analysis: join table_01 onto a week_7 slice of table_02, fit lm(ph ~ arm + age + smoker), pipe to tbl_regression().




Pick one of the four analyses and polish it for publication (axis labels, theme, panel ordering, p-value formatting, color palette).
Or, repeat the full analysis arc on nugent_score or crp_blood instead of ph. The pattern is identical; only the column name changes.



Once the room is back together: pick one result from the five analyses you built that you would be willing to put in a paper. What is the test behind it, and how would you defend that choice to a skeptical reviewer?

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
From models to reports
Yesterday we learned to model our data and interpret the outputs. Today we turn to the other half of the job: presenting those outputs so they are ready for publication.
A paper expects:

Table 1 — who was in the study
Table 2 — what differed between groups
Figures with p-values for the headline comparisons

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Goals for this module
By the end of this module you can:

report the findings of a fitted model (lm, glm, lmer) in a publication-ready table
read an analysis plan and pick the gtsummary or ggpubr call for each row
produce a Table 1 with tbl_summary() |> add_p() and override the default summary statistic and test per column
produce a Table 2 (outcome by arm) and the matching boxplot with stat_compare_means()
recognise when a paired test is the right test
report an adjusted analysis with lm() |> tbl_regression()

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
The analysis plan comes first
An analysis plan is the list of questions you want to ask your data, written down before you touch R. Each row is one question.
What would you want to know about a randomized trial like this one?

Who is in the study?
Did randomization balance the two arms?
Does the outcome differ between arms?
Did the outcome change within a person, baseline vs week 7?
Does the effect hold after adjusting for age or smoking?


Each of these is one row in the plan, and each maps to a single gtsummary or ggpubr call. The rest of the module walks them in order.

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
section: Refine your plan with an LLM
text:
Refine your plan with an LLM
Before you write any code, paste your analysis plan into a chat with an LLM and ask:

which questions are ambiguous?
which comparisons did I forget?
which defaults am I accepting without thinking?
where does my plan slip into causal language without earning it?

The LLM does not know your study design, your hypotheses, or your prior literature. It can only push back on what you wrote. The plan stays yours.

The Table 1 above used median (IQR) by default. Here is each summary drawn on two of the columns we will work with.

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Distribution drives two decisions
The decision to describe a column as median (IQR) vs mean (SD) is the same decision as choosing Wilcoxon vs t-test. Both follow from how skewed the column is.

skewed continuous → median (IQR) + Wilcoxon
symmetric continuous → mean (SD) + t-test
sparse categorical (small cells) → counts (%) + Fisher exact
dense categorical → counts (%) + chi-squared

gtsummary lets you set both with parallel statistic = list(...) and test = list(...) arguments.

Same idea, multiple outcomes at once

cytokines_keep <- c("IL-1a", "IL-6", "IL-8", "IL-1b", "MIG", "IP-10")

cytokine_panel_df <- table_03 |>
  filter(cytokine %in% cytokines_keep, limits == "within limits") |>

  filter(time_point == "week_7")

  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ cytokine, scales = "free_y") +
  stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", label.x = 1.3) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")


Six cytokines, one figure, one Wilcoxon p-value per panel.

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Multiple panels means multiple tests
Six panels means six p-values. Each is a separate hypothesis test.
At α = 0.05, expecting one false positive out of six by chance alone is normal.
Two standard corrections follow.

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Wait, what is a p-value?
We have been collecting p-values for a few slides now. Before we correct them, turn to your neighbour: what does a p-value actually tell you?
A few claims to argue about:

the probability that the null hypothesis is true
the probability the result happened by chance
the probability of seeing data this extreme if the null hypothesis were true
the probability that the treatment works

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Two ways to correct
Bonferroni multiplies each p-value by the number of tests. Strict: controls the chance of any false positive.
Benjamini-Hochberg (FDR) controls the proportion of false positives among the calls you make. More tolerant: appropriate when you expect some real effects in a screen.
Base R: p.adjust(p_values, method = "bonferroni") and p.adjust(p_values, method = "BH").

title: gtsummary and ggpubr for hypothesis testing
text:
Applied to the cytokine panel

cytokine_p <- cytokine_panel_df |>
  group_by(cytokine) |>
  summarise(p_value = wilcox.test(conc ~ arm)$p.value)

cytokine_p |>
  mutate(
    p_bonferroni = p.adjust(p_value, method = "bonferroni"),
    p_fdr        = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  )

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  cytokine   p_value p_bonferroni    p_fdr
  <chr>        <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1 IL-1a    0.0000319     0.000192 0.000192
2 IL-1b    0.000560      0.00336  0.00168 
3 IL-6     0.00740       0.0444   0.00887 
4 IL-8     0.0117        0.0699   0.0117  
5 IP-10    0.00250       0.0150   0.00374 
6 MIG      0.00114       0.00687  0.00229 


Which cytokines survive correction is the result worth reporting.
For a 6-cytokine screen, BH is usually the right choice. Use Bonferroni when even a single false positive would be costly.

Each line is one participant’s trajectory from baseline to week 7. Same data as the boxplot a few slides back. Different question: instead of comparing two groups, we are looking at change within each person.

text:
Paired pre-post: the test changes too

ggplot(pre_post_df, aes(time_point, ph)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = pid), alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_point(aes(color = arm), size = 2) +
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +
  stat_compare_means(
    method = "wilcox.test",
    paired = TRUE,
    comparisons = list(c("baseline", "week_7"))
  ) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)


paired = TRUE tells stat_compare_means() that each row at “baseline” pairs with the same participant’s row at “week_7”. The test is a paired Wilcoxon (signed-rank).
The data did not change. The unit of comparison did — each participant’s delta is now the unit. So the test changed too.

text:
The analysis plan, recap

one outcome, two groups, cross-sectional → tbl_summary + add_p or ggboxplot + stat_compare_means
many outcomes, two groups → facet_wrap + stat_compare_means
same person pre vs post → paired test on a line plot
adjust for a covariate → lm + tbl_regression
report any fitted model (lm, glm, lmer, …) → tbl_regression(fit)

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
The study
A randomized controlled trial in 51 women. Everyone received a course of antibiotics; half were randomized to eat yogurt daily, half kept their usual diet.
Each woman was sampled twice — once at baseline, once after the antibiotic course — and three kinds of measurement were taken from each sample:

qPCR — absolute load of total bacteria, L. crispatus, and L. iners
Luminex — concentrations of 10 cytokines (inflammation markers)
participant metadata — age, contraception, education

The question: does yogurt shape how the vaginal microbiome recovers from antibiotics?

qPCR spans many orders of magnitude, so we always read it on a log scale.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
section: Which cytokines can we actually use?
text: Which cytokines can we actually use?

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
Three questions

After antibiotics, do lactobacilli rebound, and does yogurt change the rebound?
Does the antibiotic course change IL-1a, and does the effect depend on the diet arm?
Across all cytokines, which ones shift from before to after?

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
The question
After a course of antibiotics, total bacterial load drops sharply. The clinically interesting question is what grows back.
L. iners and L. crispatus are the “good” lactobacilli associated with a healthy vaginal environment. Do they rebound after antibiotics, and does eating yogurt change how much they rebound?
We compare each woman to herself (baseline vs after), separately within each arm, with a paired Wilcoxon test.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
The code
qpcr_long |>
  ggplot(aes(time_point, copies + 1)) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(fill = time_point), outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(group = pid), alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_grid(arm ~ target) +
  scale_y_log10(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.05, 0.15))) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  stat_compare_means(method = "wilcox.test", paired = TRUE,
                     label = "p.format", size = 4) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gene copies / mL (log scale)")
A paired test pairs each woman’s after sample with her own baseline sample, so we measure within-person change, not differences between people.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text: The figure

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
What it means

Total bacteria fall after antibiotics, as expected.
L. iners blooms — its median jumps roughly four orders of magnitude in both arms (p < 0.001). This is the dominant recovery signal.
L. crispatus is undetectable in most women at both timepoints, so its test is underpowered.
The rebound looks the same with or without yogurt: the after boxes sit at the same height in both rows.

The headline: antibiotics clear the field and L. iners repopulates it — yogurt does not visibly steer that process.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
The question
L. iners came back. Did inflammation come down with it?
IL-1a is the best-detected cytokine here, so we model it directly. We want two things at once: the change after antibiotics, and whether that change differs by arm. That calls for an interaction model, with a per-participant random effect because each woman appears twice.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
text:
The code
il1 <- cyt |> filter(cytokine == "IL-1a")

fit <- lmer(
  log(conc) ~ arm + arm:time_point + (1 | pid),
  data = il1
)

tbl_regression(fit, intercept = TRUE)
arm:time_point lets the after-antibiotic change be different in each arm. (1 | pid) says the two samples from one woman are correlated. We model log(conc) because cytokine measurement error is multiplicative.

Reading the coefficients on the log scale:

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome

What we found

Antibiotics drop total bacterial load; L. iners repopulates strongly.
Inflammation subsides alongside that recovery, across the cytokine panel.
Yogurt left no visible fingerprint on either process in this trial.

title: Yogurt & the vaginal microbiome
section: A caveat and a next step
text:
A caveat and a next step

Depo-Provera was imbalanced between arms; a fair yogurt comparison should adjust for it.
Everything here used only the workshop’s own toolkit — tidyverse, gtsummary, ggpubr, and lme4 — assembled with an LLM assistant. The judgement about which test, which scale, and what it means stayed with us.

Tidyverse Note
tidyverse is a meta-package. Loading it also loads the core packages commonly used throughout the course, including ggplot2, dplyr, tidyr, readr, purrr, tibble, stringr, and forcats.
Because the course often uses library(tidyverse), individual tidyverse member packages may be used without appearing separately as library(ggplot2) or library(dplyr) in every file.
The interactive cheatsheet surfaces the member packages that learners actually meet through function names, so ggplot2, readr, tidyr, forcats, tibble, and stringr are not hidden under the tidyverse umbrella.

survival is still detected in Module 5 notes.qmd, even though the updated Exercise 1 no longer asks about survival models.
purrr appears in Module 5 helper code. It is listed for transparency, but can remain outside the main participant learning path unless iteration is added as a teaching topic.
MASS, lme4, and lmerTest are modeling-specific packages that may need extra attention during setup checks.
countdown is used broadly in slides, so slide rendering can fail even when the analysis packages are installed correctly.

title: From Reads to Count Tables

This afternoon
We won’t run any software today.

By the end of the afternoon you should be able to explain, in your own words, where each number in a count table came from.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
A sequencer returns text
@A00984:412:HTKJ7DSXX:1:1101:2645:1000 1:N:0:ACTGAGCG
TACGTAGGGTGCGAGCGTTGTCCGGATTTATTGGGCGTAAAGCGCGCGCAGGCGGTTTGTT
+
FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF:FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF,FFF

Each sample produces millions of these records: a read name, the sequence, and a quality score for every base.


All the processing after this tries to answer what was in the tube, and how much of it?

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
Not every base is trustworthy

Quality drops toward the end of each read. Before any counting, someone trimmed off the low-quality ends.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: The decisions already made for you
text:
The decisions already made for you
By the time you receive a count table, someone has chosen:

where to trim each read
which samples were too poor to keep
which reference to compare against
what to do with reads that matched more than one thing
what to do with reads that matched nothing


You won’t find these choices in the table, but each one changed its numbers, so ask who made them.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Both pipelines end in a count table
text:
Both pipelines end in a count table

The lab work and the software differ at every step. Both end with features in rows, samples in columns, and read counts in the cells.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
16S: one gene, every bacterium


The 16S ribosomal RNA gene is in every bacterium, and parts of it differ between species.

amplify one variable region with PCR
sequence only that amplicon
group identical sequences together
look each one up in a reference database

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
PCR distorts the proportions

Primers bind some templates better than others, and 16S copy number varies between species, so the most common species in the reads may not be the most common in the tube.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
Grouping reads: ASVs and OTUs


If two reads differ by one base, did they come from one organism or two?

OTUs cluster anything within some cutoff of each other, say 3%. Errors get absorbed, and so do close relatives.
ASVs model the sequencing error process and keep exact sequences. They can separate close relatives, if the error model is right.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Classification often stops short of species
text:
Classification often stops short of species
The sequenced region is short, and some species are identical across it.









what the classifier can say
how our table names it




Lactobacillus crispatus
lactobacillus_crispatus


Gardnerella, but which species is ambiguous
gardnerella_swidsinskii_leopoldii


family only

bacteria

Two of our 220 row names admit this uncertainty in the name itself, so read the row names before you interpret them.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: A 16S count is a number of reads
text:
A 16S count is a number of reads
A cell in the species table is the number of amplicon reads in this sample that matched this species.

It is not the number of bacteria. The count also depends on

how many copies of the 16S gene that species carries
how well the primers bind to it
how completely the cells lysed
how deeply the sample was sequenced

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
RNA-seq: every gene, one organism



pull out messenger RNA
copy it to cDNA and fragment it
sequence the fragments
find where each fragment belongs in the genome
count fragments overlapping each gene

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: An RNA-seq count is a number of fragments
text:
An RNA-seq count is a number of fragments
A cell in the gene table is the number of fragments in this sample assigned to this gene.

It is not the number of mRNA molecules either. The count also depends on

how long the gene is
how well the capture chemistry worked
whether the read could be placed uniquely
how deeply the sample was sequenced

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
One swab, two experiments
A cervicovaginal swab contains human cells and bacteria together.

The 16S run amplifies a bacterial gene, so human material is mostly ignored.
The RNA-seq run captures polyadenylated RNA, which is mostly human.
Neither table is pure, but both come from the same swab.


Because they share a swab, we can pair the two tables sample by sample.

section: Some reads fit more than one gene
text:
Some reads fit more than one gene

Gene families and repeated sequences produce reads that match several genes equally well. Counting such a read once, twice, or not at all gives a different table each time.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
Counts, not TPM, for testing
You will see expression reported as TPM, FPKM or RPKM. Those divide by gene length so you can compare genes within a sample.

Good for: “is gene A higher than gene B in this sample?”
Wrong for: the statistical tests we run on Wednesday


Those tests need raw counts, because they model counting noise. Hand them normalised values and they will believe the noise is smaller than it is.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: When C grows, A and B appear to shrink
text:
When C grows, A and B appear to shrink

A and B have 100 cells in both samples, but their share of the reads falls from a third to a ninth.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Both of our tables are compositional
text:
Both of our tables are compositional



16S is hit hardest, because one species routinely holds 90% of the reads.
RNA-seq is affected less, since no single gene dominates, but the effect is still there.

“Relative abundance went down” and “there was less of it” are different claims. Without a spike-in or an absolute measurement, you cannot tell them apart.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
Ask your sequencing facility for

the raw reads, not just the table
the exact reference and version used
which samples failed and were re-run
which plate, run and lane each sample sat on
the negative and positive controls, with their counts


The controls are how you catch contamination, and few people ask for them.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Common problems and how to spot them
text:
Common problems and how to spot them







problem
how you notice




contamination from reagents
the same taxa in your negative controls


low-biomass samples
tiny library sizes, odd composition


index hopping between samples
a trace of everything in everything


a batch effect
samples cluster by run, not by biology




You can only see three of these four if somebody recorded the metadata.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
text:
The sentence to remember
A count measures how much of something was in the tube relative to everything else in that tube, multiplied by how hard we looked.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Every analysis starts the same way
text:
Every analysis starts the same way

How deeply was each sample sequenced?
Which features are we even able to see?
How alike are whole samples, and what makes them alike?
Only then: which features differ between groups?


Tomorrow morning covers the first two, on both tables at once, and tomorrow afternoon the third. The fourth waits until Wednesday.

title: From Reads to Count Tables
section: Our gene table has a batch label
text:
Our gene table has a batch label
The gene table was produced in two sequencing batches, and we kept that label in the metadata.

Tomorrow afternoon you will measure how much of the table the batch explains, and the answer is uncomfortable.


Keep every technical label your sequencing facility gives you. A batch effect you never recorded is one you cannot test for.

title: Distances and Ordination
section: From one feature to whole samples
text:
From one feature to whole samples
This morning you looked at one sample or one feature at a time. This afternoon the question is how similar two whole samples are.

That gives one number per pair of samples, and then a picture of all of them at once.

title: Distances and Ordination
text:
A distance matrix

This toy has 12 samples. Ours has 471, which makes 110,685 pairs. The diagonal is zero, the matrix is symmetric, and there is nothing else in it.

title: Differential Testing
text:
The question
For each feature, is its count systematically different between two groups of samples?

In the gene table we ask it about 14,000 times, once per gene.

title: Differential Testing
section: Counts break the assumptions of a t-test
text:
Counts break the assumptions of a t-test



Counts can’t go below zero, and they are skewed.
The variance depends on the mean: a gene at 10 counts behaves differently from one at 10,000.
Library sizes differ, so raw counts aren’t comparable between samples.
Estimating each gene’s variance on its own, from 157 samples, ignores what the other 14,000 genes can tell you.

title: Differential Testing
section: The variance really does track the mean
text:
The variance really does track the mean

Fold changes for low-count genes are much less certain. A method built for counts uses this trend to borrow information across genes.

title: Differential Testing
text:
Running DESeq2

library(DESeq2)

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = gene_counts,          # features x samples, raw counts
  colData   = sample_table,         # one row per sample, same order
  design    = ~ community
)

dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("community", "anaerobe", "lactobacillus"))


Give it raw counts, never CPM and never logged values. DESeq2 does its own normalisation, and feeding it normalised data breaks it.

title: Differential Testing
text:
Three things distort a count










gene table

comparing one feature across samples

some samples sequenced deeper
the same
matters


feature yield
long genes collect more fragments
16S copy number, primer fit
cancels, because a gene is the same length in every sample


composition
a few genes take up the reads
one species often takes 90% of them
matters, most of all for species




Differential testing compares one feature across samples, so it has to handle depth and composition. That is the job of the size factor, and it is why the size factor is not simply the library size.


Length does matter when you compare two genes inside one sample. That is what TPM is for, and it is not what we are doing today.

title: Differential Testing
text:
Inside DESeq()

Size factors. One number per sample that puts the samples on a common scale, correcting for depth and composition.
Dispersion. Estimates each feature’s variance, then pulls extreme estimates toward the trend you just saw.
Test. Fits a model per feature and tests whether the group term is zero.

title: Sets and Enrichment
section: A gene list is hard to report
text:
A gene list is hard to report

You cannot read 1,698 names
You cannot put them in an abstract
Two groups with the same data will hand you two different lists


You need to say what the genes have in common.

title: Sets and Enrichment
text:
Cut-off tests and ranked tests



Cut, then count. Take your significant genes and a predefined set, and ask whether the overlap is bigger than chance (a hypergeometric test). It is simple, and it ignores every gene below your cutoff.
Rank, then look. Order every gene you tested from most up to most down, and ask whether a set’s members pile up at one end. This needs no cutoff. It is called gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).


We use GSEA, because with the first approach the answer depends on a threshold you picked arbitrarily.

title: Sets and Enrichment
section: A gene set is a named list
text:
A gene set is a named list


Someone curated it, from papers or experiments.

We use the Hallmark collection: 50 sets of about 200 genes, one for each broad biological program.

title: Sets and Enrichment
text:
Check the tail every time
Before you believe an enrichment, sort your genes by the size of their effect and look at the top few hundred.

If those nearly all point one way, every large set will come out enriched that way, and the method will give you a very small p-value for it.


Our community ranking was centred overall and still failed this check.

Sets overlap. TNFA signalling and inflammatory response share many genes, so their p-values are not independent and you cannot count them as separate findings.
People curated them, mostly from experiments in cell lines and mostly not from cervical tissue.
If nobody has curated a set for the biology you study, enrichment cannot find it.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together

text:
So far, one table at a time

We ran every method this week twice, once on each table, and never on both together.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
Today’s question
Does putting the two tables together tell you anything that neither told you alone?

Sometimes, and you can measure when.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
When combining helps

If both tables carry the same information, combining them adds nothing beyond a slightly better estimate of that one thing.
If they carry different information, combining them can add a lot.
If one carries nothing, combining them makes your model worse, because you spent degrees of freedom on noise.


So before fitting any model, measure how much the two tables already agree.

# from the gene table: how inflamed, using Thursday's gene set

scores in one model
Reduce each table to a few numbers and fit one model, as we did today. Every other method has to beat this.


intermediate
canonical correlation, PLS, sparse PLS
Find the combination of features in table A that best tracks a combination in table B.


multi-block
DIABLO, MOFA
Decompose several tables at once into shared and table-specific factors.


similarity-based
Procrustes, co-inertia, DiSTATIS
Compare the sample configurations rather than the features.


networks

Build a graph across data types and look at its structure.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
All of them can overfit
With 157 people and 14,446 features, you can find a combination that separates your groups perfectly.

It will not replicate.


Every method on that list needs cross-validation or a held-out set, and the fancier the method the more it needs it.

title: Putting the Two Tables Together
text:
Our own result, honestly stated



We chose both scores after looking at the data all week.
We never held out a test set.
AUC 0.84 with a 95% interval of 0.78 to 0.91.
The two intervals for the single-table models overlap each other.













The improvement is real, but we should be modest about how big it is, and say both when we report it.

Thirty minutes to finish preparing. Then each Study A group pairs with the Study B group of the same number: A1 presents to B1 for 30 minutes, then B1 presents to A1.

Tell the other group what you asked, what you found, and what you do not believe about your own result.
